questions.stem: How does Viola arrive in Illyria?
options: She is shipwrecked and believes her twin brother has drowned
She runs away from home to escape a marriage to Orsino
She is sent by her father to serve as Olivia's companion
She is shipwrecked with Sebastian, and the two are rescued together
questions.explanation: Viola is rescued by a sea captain after a storm. She fears her twin, Sebastian, is drowned, and decides to serve Duke Orsino disguised as a young man.

questions.stem: What name does Viola take while disguised as a young man?
options: Valentine
Cesario
Sebastian
Antonio
questions.explanation: As Cesario, Viola quickly becomes Orsino's favourite servant. Sebastian is her twin; Antonio is his rescuer; Valentine is one of Orsino's gentlemen.

questions.stem: Why does Olivia refuse to see Orsino or any suitor at the start of the play?
options: She has secretly promised to marry Sir Andrew Aguecheek
She has taken a vow to enter a convent outside Illyria
She is mourning her husband, who has recently been lost at sea
She is mourning the recent deaths of her father and brother
questions.explanation: Olivia has vowed to hide herself away and mourn her brother for seven years. Feste soon teases her that it is foolish to mourn a brother whose soul is in heaven.

questions.stem: What goes wrong when Orsino sends Cesario to woo Olivia for him?
options: Olivia accepts Orsino's offer, and Viola must arrange their wedding
Olivia sees through the disguise and tells Orsino that Cesario is a woman
Olivia sends Cesario away, and Orsino dismisses Viola from his service
Olivia falls in love with Cesario, while Viola herself loves Orsino
questions.explanation: Viola loves Orsino, Orsino loves Olivia, and Olivia loves Cesario. The love triangle, which only the audience fully understands, drives the comedy.

questions.stem: How does Olivia let Cesario know she has fallen in love with him?
options: She writes Cesario a love letter in her own hand, which Maria delivers
She gives Feste a song to sing to Cesario at Orsino's house
She sends Malvolio after Cesario with a ring she claims Cesario left
She sends Feste after Cesario with a ring she claims Cesario left
questions.explanation: Cesario left no ring. Viola works out what it means in her soliloquy 'I am the man', realising that her disguise has caused a lady to fall for her.

questions.stem: Why do Sir Toby, Maria and the others plot against Malvolio?
options: He has tried to have Feste dismissed from Olivia's house for being drunk on duty
He scolds them for their late-night drinking and singing, and threatens to tell Olivia
He has caught Maria forging Olivia's handwriting and reported her to Olivia
He has refused to pay Sir Toby's debts out of Olivia's money, as Toby demanded
questions.explanation: Malvolio breaks up the revelry in Act 2, Scene 3, and Toby answers with the famous line about cakes and ale. Maria then plans to forge a love letter in Olivia's handwriting.

questions.stem: What does the forged letter tell Malvolio to do?
options: Wear yellow stockings, be cross-gartered and smile
Dress in black and stay silent in Olivia's presence
Challenge Cesario to a duel to prove his courage
Sing love songs beneath Olivia's window each night
questions.explanation: The letter seems to say that Olivia loves him. Malvolio obeys, appearing in yellow stockings, cross-gartered and smiling, things Olivia actually hates, and she thinks he has gone mad.

questions.stem: What happens to Malvolio after he appears before Olivia in yellow stockings?
options: Maria confesses the trick and he forgives everyone
Sir Toby has him locked in a dark room as a madman
Olivia dismisses him and he leaves Illyria at once
Sir Andrew challenges him to a duel over Olivia
questions.explanation: Locking the mad in darkness was a common treatment at the time. Feste, disguised as the curate Sir Topas, visits him and insists he is mad, which pushes the joke into cruelty.

questions.stem: Why does Antonio feel betrayed when he rescues Cesario from the duel?
options: He thinks Cesario is Sebastian, who now seems to deny knowing him
He learns that Cesario is the servant of the Duke who imprisoned him
He discovers that Cesario has stolen the purse he gave to Sebastian
He realises that Cesario has told the officers where to find him
questions.explanation: Antonio, arrested by Orsino's officers, asks 'Sebastian' for his purse back. Viola has never met him, but hearing her brother's name gives her hope that Sebastian is alive.

questions.stem: Why does Olivia marry Sebastian in Act 4?
options: Sir Toby arranges it to stop her marrying Orsino
She mistakes him for Cesario, and he gladly agrees
She knows he is Sebastian and prefers him to Cesario
She learns he is Viola's brother and wants a noble match
questions.explanation: Sebastian, puzzled but delighted, follows Olivia to a priest and is betrothed to her. He agrees, saying that 'having sworn truth', he 'ever will be true'.

questions.stem: How is the confusion resolved in the final scene?
options: Antonio recognises Viola as Sebastian's sister and explains
Viola and Sebastian appear together, and the twins recognise each other
Feste explains the whole tangled plot to Orsino and Olivia in a final song
The sea captain arrives and reveals Viola's true identity
questions.explanation: Seeing them side by side, Orsino exclaims 'One face, one voice, one habit, and two persons!' The twins test each other's memories before rejoicing, and the couples sort themselves out.

questions.stem: How does Malvolio leave the play?
options: Accepting Olivia's apology and returning to his duties
Marrying Maria after she confesses she wrote the letter
Swearing 'I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you!'
Forgiving everyone and dancing at the double wedding
questions.explanation: Freed and told of the trick, Malvolio storms off. Orsino orders that he be followed and calmed, but his exit leaves a sour note in the happy ending.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Orsino at the start of the play?
options: He is a poor duke who wants to marry Olivia mainly for her money
He is in love with the idea of love, and indulges his own melancholy
He is a decisive ruler whose love for Olivia is calm, steady and constant
He has given up on Olivia and is now looking for a new wife
questions.explanation: Orsino opens the play asking for music to feed his love until it sickens. His changeable moods suggest he loves his own feelings as much as Olivia.

questions.stem: Malvolio is best described as:
options: Olivia's proud, self-important steward, who dreams of rising above his station
Orsino's loyal servant, who carries messages of love between the Duke and Olivia
Olivia's jester, who is paid to entertain her with songs and riddles
Sir Toby's drinking companion, who is fooled into courting Olivia
questions.explanation: Olivia tells him he is 'sick of self-love'. Before he even finds the letter, he imagines himself as 'Count Malvolio', married to Olivia and giving orders to Toby.

questions.stem: Who are Sir Toby Belch and Sir Andrew Aguecheek?
options: Orsino's kinsman and a rich knight who hopes to marry Viola
Olivia's drunken uncle and a foolish knight who hopes to marry her
Orsino's two advisers, who encourage him to give up on Olivia
Olivia's drunken cousin and a soldier who is courting Maria
questions.explanation: Toby lives in his niece's house, drinking and joking. He keeps Andrew around because Andrew pays for everything, using his hopes of Olivia to drain his money.

questions.stem: What role does Feste the Fool play?
options: Orsino's household fool, sent to cheer Olivia during her mourning
A messenger who carries letters between Orsino's court and Olivia's house
A witty professional fool who sees more clearly than the nobles he serves
A simple servant who believes everything he is told and is often tricked
questions.explanation: Feste moves between Orsino's and Olivia's houses, earning money with songs and wordplay. Viola says he 'is wise enough to play the Fool', because fooling well takes wit.

questions.stem: How do Viola and Orsino differ in the way they love?
options: Viola speaks openly of her love to Orsino, while Orsino hides his love for Olivia
Viola loves patiently and silently, while Orsino's love is showy and self-absorbed
Viola loves Orsino for his rank and wealth, while Orsino loves Olivia for her wit
Viola changes the object of her love often, while Orsino stays constant throughout
questions.explanation: Viola hides her love behind her disguise and tells of a 'sister' who 'never told her love'. Orsino talks endlessly of his passion, yet transfers it to Viola within moments at the end.

questions.stem: Antonio's role is sometimes described as one of the play's loose ends. Why?
options: He rescued Viola from the wreck, but the two are not reunited at the end
He becomes Orsino's new steward at the end, but the play gives no reason why
He shows devoted love for Sebastian, but the ending gives him no place in its happiness
He loves Olivia devotedly, but she marries Sebastian and leaves him with nothing
questions.explanation: Antonio risks arrest in Orsino's territory out of love for Sebastian. In the last scene the couples pair off, and Antonio is left without a word about his future, like Malvolio an outsider to the celebration.

questions.stem: What does the title 'Twelfth Night' refer to?
options: The night of Olivia's wedding, which takes place exactly twelve days after the wreck
The twelfth night of mourning, when Olivia finally agrees to see Orsino
The last night of the Christmas season, a time of festive celebration and misrule
The twelfth night of Viola's voyage, when the ship is wrecked off the coast
questions.explanation: Twelfth Night, the eve of the Epiphany, ended the Christmas holidays with feasting, disguise and role reversal. The play's mistaken identities and upside-down social order echo that spirit of misrule.

questions.stem: In Shakespeare's theatre, women's roles were played by boys. How does this add to the comedy of Viola's disguise?
options: A grown man played Viola, so the audience laughed at his deep voice as Cesario
An adult actress played Viola, so the disguise seemed deliberately unconvincing
A boy actor played a girl disguised as a boy, layering the confusion of gender
A boy actor played Orsino, so the audience saw two boys fall in love on stage
questions.explanation: Viola was played by a boy actor, so the original audience saw a boy playing a girl playing a boy. This adds a further layer to the play's games with identity and desire.

questions.stem: Maria says of Malvolio, 'sometimes he is a kind of puritan.' What would Shakespeare's audience have understood?
options: Puritans disapproved of festivity and theatre, so Malvolio is an enemy of fun
Puritans favoured lavish dress, so Malvolio is vain about his clothes
Puritans were loyal Catholics, so Malvolio is a secret rebel
Puritans supported the theatres, so Malvolio is on the players' side
questions.explanation: Puritans opposed theatres and many traditional festivities. Making the killjoy steward 'a kind of puritan' would have appealed to an audience who loved both.

questions.stem: Illyria was a real region on the Adriatic coast. How does the play use it as a setting?
options: As a dangerous war zone where the characters must constantly defend themselves
As a distant, dreamlike place where normal rules of identity and class are loosened
As an accurate picture of a real foreign court, based on Shakespeare's own travels
As a stand-in for London, with real streets and landmarks the audience would know
questions.explanation: Viola's first question is 'What country, friends, is this?' Illyria's name may suggest illusion and delirium, and it works as a festive, faraway space where disguise and love can run free.

questions.stem: Which theme is most central to Twelfth Night?
options: The confusions of love and desire, made worse by disguise
Social ambition and its punishment, shown through Malvolio
The loyalty of siblings separated by misfortune
The conflict between parents and children over marriage
questions.explanation: Almost everyone loves the wrong person: Orsino loves Olivia, Olivia loves Cesario, Viola loves Orsino. Disguise and mistaken identity tangle these desires until the twins are reunited.

questions.stem: How does the play explore gender and identity?
options: The disguise reinforces fixed gender roles, as Viola's fear in the duel shows
The play treats identity as fixed, since everyone sees through Viola
Orsino's love shows that men feel more deeply and constantly than women
Viola's disguise lets her see love from both sides and blurs fixed gender roles
questions.explanation: As Cesario, Viola speaks to Orsino as a man and to Olivia as a suitor. Orsino calls her 'Cesario' even after the truth is out, and the play enjoys the confusion rather than tidying it away.

questions.stem: In what sense is Twelfth Night a comedy with a darker side?
options: The couples marry unwillingly, under orders from Orsino, who rules over Illyria as Duke
Viola is punished for her disguise and sent away from Orsino's court
Sebastian drowns in the storm, and Viola mourns him to the end
The joyful marriages are shadowed by Malvolio's humiliation and Antonio's exclusion
questions.explanation: The comedy ends in marriage, yet Malvolio storms out vowing revenge, Antonio has no place in the celebration, and Feste sings that 'the rain it raineth every day'. The festival is ending.

questions.stem: What does Malvolio's treatment suggest about the play's view of social class?
options: It suggests servants are wiser than their masters, as Malvolio proves
It presents his punishment as fully deserved, and the play's ending confirms that verdict
It celebrates rising in rank, as Maria and Malvolio both marry up
It mocks his ambition to rise above his station, yet his punishment seems excessive
questions.explanation: Malvolio dreams of becoming 'Count Malvolio', and the play laughs at him. But his confinement in the dark goes far beyond a joke, and even Olivia says he 'hath been most notoriously abused'.

questions.stem: What dramatic device creates most of the comedy in Twelfth Night?
options: Dramatic irony, because the audience knows who Cesario is
Situational irony, as the audience is kept guessing about Cesario
Slapstick, since most scenes are built around duels and beatings
Satire of the court, aimed at Orsino's failures as a ruler
questions.explanation: The audience knows Cesario is Viola, and later that Sebastian is alive. We enjoy watching characters misread each other, from Olivia's love to Antonio's anger.

questions.stem: What is the function of the subplot involving Malvolio and the forged letter?
options: It mirrors the main plot's themes of self-deception and misplaced love
It provides comic relief that stands apart from the play's main themes
It shows a servant's love for Olivia succeeding where Orsino's fails
It sets up the twins' reunion by delaying Sebastian's arrival
questions.explanation: Like Orsino, Malvolio loves Olivia and is deceived about her feelings, partly by his own vanity. The subplot comments on the main plot, as the box-tree scene of self-delusion echoes Orsino's.

questions.stem: What do Feste's songs add to the play?
options: They celebrate youth as something lasting, and love as easily won and easily kept
They are sung by Viola to reveal her hidden love for Orsino
They bring a note of melancholy, reminding the audience that youth and joy pass
They advance the plot by revealing to Olivia who Cesario really is
questions.explanation: Songs such as 'O mistress mine' warn that 'Youth's a stuff will not endure', and 'Come away, death' suits Orsino's mood. The final song about the rain ends the festive comedy on a wistful note.

questions.stem: Why do the comic characters, such as Toby, Andrew and Maria, mostly speak in prose?
options: Prose suits their lower-key, everyday scenes, while the lovers often speak in verse
Prose marks them as the play's most serious and thoughtful characters
Prose marks them out as the nobility, while servants such as Cesario speak in verse
Prose is used because these characters are speaking in soliloquy
questions.explanation: Shakespeare often gives romantic and noble moments to verse and comic, domestic scenes to prose. The switch helps mark the change between the love plot and the revellers' subplot.

questions.stem: In Act 3, Scene 4, Fabian says, 'If this were played upon a stage now, I could condemn it as an improbable fiction.' What is the effect?
options: It jokes about the play's own unlikely plot, drawing the audience into the fun
It warns the audience that the rest of the play will be serious and tragic
It reveals that Fabian disapproves of the trick and wants it stopped
It reveals that the trick on Malvolio was planned by Olivia from the start
questions.explanation: Fabian says this while watching Malvolio's antics. The metatheatrical joke admits the plot is far-fetched, and invites the audience to enjoy it anyway.

questions.stem: Who says 'If music be the food of love, play on'?
options: Olivia, on first meeting Cesario
Orsino, in the play's opening line
Viola, as she arrives in Illyria
Feste, before singing to Olivia
questions.explanation: Orsino's opening speech asks for so much music that his appetite for love will sicken and die. It introduces his indulgent, changeable feelings at once.

questions.stem: Viola says, 'O Time, thou must untangle this, not I. / It is too hard a knot for me t' untie.' When does she say it, and what does it show?
options: After Orsino sends her to Olivia; she is excited by the adventure
After meeting Sebastian; she is overjoyed that he survived the storm
After realising Olivia loves Cesario; she feels trapped by her disguise
After the duel with Sir Andrew; she is relieved to have escaped harm
questions.explanation: In her soliloquy in Act 2, Scene 2, Viola cannot reveal herself without losing her place with Orsino. She hands the problem to time, which, in a comedy, will indeed untangle it.

questions.stem: Sir Toby asks Malvolio, 'Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?' What conflict does this show?
options: Romantic love against the demands of family loyalty
Olivia's mourning against her wish to marry again
Wealth against poverty within Olivia's household
Festive enjoyment against Malvolio's strict disapproval
questions.explanation: Toby says this when Malvolio scolds the late-night revellers in Act 2, Scene 3. The line sums up the clash between festive pleasure and puritanical restraint.

questions.stem: Malvolio reads, 'Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.' Why is the line comic?
options: Malvolio is mocking Sir Toby, who was born to greatness
Malvolio believes greatness is about to be thrust on him, though it is a trick
Malvolio reads it aloud to Olivia, who is secretly listening to him
Malvolio realises at once that the letter is forged and decides to play along
questions.explanation: Reading the forged letter in Act 2, Scene 5, Malvolio takes it as proof that Olivia wants to raise him up. The line is repeated back to him at the end, when he learns the truth.

questions.stem: In Act 3, Scene 1, Viola tells Olivia, 'I am not what I am.' What makes the line so rich in meaning?
options: It is a lie meant to make Olivia believe that Cesario is really a nobleman in disguise
It is a direct confession of her disguise, which Olivia understands at once
It is a joke at Malvolio's expense, which Olivia enjoys
It is literally true, as she is a woman in disguise, but Olivia misses the meaning
questions.explanation: The audience hears a sincere hint at the truth; Olivia hears only a riddle. The line captures the play's dramatic irony about identity.

questions.stem: Feste's final speech ends, 'And thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenges.' What does it suggest?
options: That time turns things round, so Malvolio's insults come back on him
That Feste plans to take revenge on Orsino for refusing him payment
That Olivia will come to regret her hasty marriage to Sebastian
That Malvolio's revenge will soon fall on Sir Toby and Maria
questions.explanation: Feste reminds Malvolio of his earlier sneers at the Fool. The spinning top of the 'whirligig' suggests fortune and time turning, which leads straight to Malvolio's angry exit.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt ''Twelfth Night shows that love makes fools of everyone.' Discuss.'?
options: In Twelfth Night, Orsino loves Olivia, Olivia loves Cesario, and Viola is in love with Orsino
Shakespeare suggests that love leads almost every character into folly, though Viola's love is wiser
Twelfth Night is a comedy written by William Shakespeare around 1601 for performance in London
This essay will discuss all the different characters who fall in love in Twelfth Night by Shakespeare
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and signals a qualification. The others give facts, announce the essay or retell the plot.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Malvolio wears yellow stockings and smiles at Olivia.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Explain how his costume shows his vanity making him blind to the obvious trick
Add which act and scene it happens in and who else is standing on the stage with him
Describe what colour Olivia's own clothes are in the same scene
List all the other instructions that were written in the forged letter
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence shows. Linking the costume to Malvolio's self-love connects the moment to the play's ideas about self-deception and social ambition.
